content: 1. In cases of life-threatening, severe, or overwhelming malaria infections caused by Plasmodium falciparum, patients should be treated with an intravenous antimalarial drug. After completing the intravenous treatment, mefloquine may be administered to complete the therapy. 2. Mefloquine should not be co-administered with halofantrine or given within 15 weeks of the last dose of halofantrine due to the risk of potentially fatal QTc interval prolongation. 3. Ketoconazole should not be administered with mefloquine or within 15 weeks of the last dose of mefloquine because it increases plasma concentrations and the elimination half-life of mefloquine, which can lead to a potentially fatal prolongation of the QTc interval. 4. Concomitant administration of mefloquine with quinine or quinidine may result in electrocardiographic abnormalities. 5. Mefloquine can cause neuropsychiatric adverse reactions in both adults and children. Neuropsychiatric symptoms in children, especially nonverbal ones, may be difficult to identify, necessitating close monitoring. 6. Psychiatric symptoms associated with mefloquine use can range from anxiety, paranoia, and depression to hallucinations and psychotic behavior. These symptoms may occur early in the course of treatment and, in some cases, persist for months or years after discontinuation of the drug. Suicidal ideation and suicide have also been reported. 7. Mefloquine should not be prescribed for prophylaxis in patients with active depression, generalized anxiety disorder, psychosis, schizophrenia, or other major psychiatric disorders. It should be used cautiously in patients with a history of depression. 8. During prophylactic use, the emergence of psychiatric symptoms such as acute anxiety, depression, restlessness, or confusion may indicate a risk of more severe psychiatric or neurologic adverse reactions. In such cases, the drug should be discontinued, and an alternative medication should be used. 9. Neurologic symptoms such as dizziness, vertigo, tinnitus, and loss of balance have been reported with mefloquine use. These symptoms may occur early in treatment and, in some cases, persist for months or years after discontinuation. In rare cases, these symptoms may be permanent. 10. If neurologic symptoms occur during prophylactic use, the drug should be discontinued, and an alternative medication should be substituted. Patients should exercise caution with activities requiring alertness and fine motor coordination, such as driving, piloting aircraft, operating machinery, or deep-sea diving, while symptoms persist. 11. Mefloquine may increase the risk of seizures in patients with epilepsy. It should only be prescribed for curative treatment in such patients if there are compelling medical reasons for its use. 12. Concomitant administration of mefloquine with quinine or chloroquine may increase the risk of seizures. 13. Hypersensitivity reactions have been reported with mefloquine use. 14. In patients with impaired liver function, the elimination of mefloquine may be prolonged, leading to higher plasma levels and an increased risk of adverse reactions. 15. Mefloquine has been administered for periods longer than one year. For prolonged use, periodic evaluations, including liver function tests and assessments for neuropsychiatric effects, should be performed. Periodic ophthalmic examinations are also recommended. 16. Mefloquine is a myocardial depressant and has been shown in animal studies to possess 20% of the anti-fibrillatory action of quinidine and produce 50% of the increase in PR interval reported with quinine. Its effects on compromised cardiovascular systems have not been evaluated, but transient and clinically silent ECG alterations, such as sinus bradycardia, sinus arrhythmia, first-degree AV block, QTc interval prolongation, and abnormal T waves, have been reported. 17. The benefits of mefloquine therapy should be weighed against the potential for adverse effects in patients with cardiac disease. 18. Resistance to mefloquine by Plasmodium falciparum has been reported, particularly in areas of multidrug resistance in Southeast Asia. Cross-resistance between mefloquine and halofantrine, as well as between mefloquine and quinine, has been observed in some regions. 19. Cases of agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia have been reported with mefloquine use. 20. During prolonged prophylaxis, periodic evaluation of hepatic function is recommended. 21. Patients should be provided with a Medication Guide and an information wallet card when mefloquine is dispensed. They should be instructed to read the Medication Guide and carry the wallet card while taking mefloquine. 22. Patients should be informed that malaria is a life-threatening infection and that mefloquine is prescribed to help prevent or treat this serious condition. However, some patients may be unable to tolerate the medication due to side effects, such as dizziness, vertigo, or loss of balance, which may persist for months or years after discontinuation and, in some cases, may be permanent. 23. Patients should be advised that insomnia may occur with mefloquine use. 24. When used for prophylaxis, the first dose of mefloquine should be taken one week prior to arrival in a malaria-endemic area. 25. If psychiatric adverse reactions such as acute anxiety, depression, restlessness, confusion, or suicidal ideation occur, the drug should be discontinued, and an alternative medication should be used. 26. Patients should be reminded that no chemoprophylactic regimen is 100% effective and that protective clothing, insect repellents, and bed nets are important components of malaria prevention. 27. Patients should seek medical attention for any febrile illness that occurs after returning from a malaria-endemic area and inform their physician of possible malaria exposure.
